answers.t: Sino ang nagluto sa party? Ano ang ginawa mo noong Sabado?
answers.tr: Who cooked at the party? What did you do on Saturday?

answers.t: Sino ang sumama sa iyo sa beach? Ano ang kinain ninyo?
answers.tr: Who went to the beach with you? What did you eat?

lessons.title: Use English words the Tagalog way
lessons.summary: Do what Manila does every day and put English words into Tagalog sentences: “Text me later.” “I already sent it.” “I got stuck in traffic.”
lessons.topic: Taglish verbs: {{mag-}} + English ({{mag-text}}), {{i-}} + English ({{i-send}}), {{na-}} + English ({{na-late}}), with the forms you know

dialog.t: Oo, pero hindi pa siya nagre-reply.
dialog.tr: Yes, but he hasn't replied yet.

dialog.t: Baka busy siya. I-send mo na lang sa akin ang address.
dialog.tr: Maybe he's busy. Just send me the address.

blocks.p: Manila Tagalog borrows English words all the time, above all for phones, work and school, and it bends them with the same pieces you already know. The mix is called **Taglish**. It's normal everyday speech, not a mistake, though formal Tagalog (the news, speeches) avoids it.

**Doing something (actor focus)**: {{mag-}} + the English word: {{mag-text}} “text”, {{mag-drive}} “drive”, {{mag-shopping}} “go shopping”, {{mag-enjoy}} “have a good time”. Its forms work exactly like {{magluto}}, repeating the first sounds of the English word.

**Doing it to a particular thing (object focus)**: {{i-}} + the English word: {{i-send}} “send (it)”, {{i-check}} “check (it)”, {{i-save}}, {{i-print}}. {{I-send mo sa akin.}} “Send it to me.” Once done, people usually say {{sinend}}, {{chineck}}: {{Sinend ko na.}} “I've already sent it.” Not yet begun: {{i-se-send}}, {{i-che-check}}.

**Something that happened to you**: {{na-}} + the English word: {{na-late}} “was late”, {{na-traffic}} “got stuck in traffic”, {{na-stress}} “got stressed”. {{Na-traffic ako.}} “I got stuck in traffic.” (Lesson 45 explains this {{na-}}.)

ex.tr: We got stuck in traffic on EDSA.
Did you have a good time?

blocks.tip: Taglish spelling is loose: you'll see {{i-text}} and {{itext}}, {{nag-text}} and {{nagtext}}. Write it as you like; what matters is saying it with the Tagalog pattern.

mistakes.why: The person you text takes {{sa}}: {{sa iyo}} “to you”.
{{i-send}} is the basic form; yesterday it was done, so the completed form, {{sinend}}.

practice.q: You arrive late because of the traffic. You say…
A coworker asks about a report. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Tapos mo na ba ang report?

lines.why: Earlier: already done, so {{sinend}}.

lines.t: Talaga? I-che-check ko ang email ko.

lines.why: A command about a particular thing: {{i-check mo}}.

practice.q: Your turn: tell a friend about your day in Taglish: something you texted, sent or checked, and something that happened to you.

answers.t: Nag-text ako kay Mama. Sinend ko ang report. Na-late ako sa meeting.
answers.tr: I texted Mom. I sent the report. I was late for the meeting.

answers.t: Na-traffic ako kanina, pero nag-enjoy ako sa party.
answers.tr: I got stuck in traffic earlier, but I had a good time at the party.

lessons.title: Tell someone what you did yesterday
lessons.summary: Tell what happened, step by step: “On Saturday we went to Tagaytay. Then Ana bought a buko pie and we ate it in the car!”
lessons.topic: The completed forms of every focus, one after another; {{una}}, {{tapos}}, {{pagkatapos}}; {{kahapon}}, {{kagabi}}, {{kanina}}, {{noong}}

goal.t: Pumunta ako sa palengke kahapon, tapos nagluto ako.
goal.tr: I went to the market yesterday, then I cooked.

dialog.t: Ano ang ginawa mo noong Sabado?
dialog.tr: What did you do on Saturday?

dialog.t: Pumunta kami sa Tagaytay. Kumain kami ng bulalo.
dialog.tr: We went to Tagaytay. We had bulalo.

dialog.t: Tapos, bumili si Ana ng buko pie, at kinain namin sa kotse!
dialog.tr: Then Ana bought a buko pie, and we ate it in the car!

blocks.p: Telling what happened means using the **completed** forms one after another, each with the focus that fits: {{Pumunta kami}} (we went), {{bumili si Ana ng buko pie}} (Ana bought a pie: just “a pie”), {{kinain namin}} (we ate it: that particular pie, so object focus).
**In order**: {{una}} “first”, {{tapos}} “then” (the everyday word), {{pagkatapos}} “after that”, {{saka}} “and then”. {{Una, naligo ako. Tapos, nag-almusal ako.}}

**When**: {{kahapon}} “yesterday”, {{kagabi}} “last night”, {{kanina}} “earlier today” ({{kaninang umaga}} “this morning”), {{noong Sabado}} “on Saturday”, {{noong isang linggo}} “last week”. A time word often starts the story: {{Kahapon, pumunta ako…}}
**Keeping the listener with you**: listeners say {{Tapos?}} “And then?” or {{Talaga?}} “Really?”; you can start with {{Alam mo,…}} “You know what,…”

ex.t: Pumunta ako sa palengke kahapon, tapos nagluto ako.
ex.tr: I went to the market yesterday, then I cooked.
Last night we went to the movies.

ex.t: Kaninang umaga, tinawagan ko si Lola.
Una, naligo ako. Tapos, nag-almusal ako.
ex.tr: First I showered. Then I had breakfast.

ex.t: Noong isang linggo, pumunta kami sa Cebu.
ex.tr: Last week we went to Cebu.

blocks.tip: {{kanina}} is earlier **today**; {{kahapon}} is yesterday. {{kaninang umaga}} “this morning” is said later the same day.

mistakes.tr: Yesterday I went to the market.
mistakes.why: Yesterday, finished: the completed form.
Just some bulalo: actor focus. For that particular bowl, {{Kinain ko ang bulalo}}.

mistakes.wrong: Kanina gabi, nanood kami ng sine.
mistakes.tr: Last night we watched a movie.
mistakes.why: “Last night” is one word, {{kagabi}}; {{kanina}} is earlier today.

practice.tr: Last night we watched a movie.

practice.why: Grandma is in focus, the call is done: {{tinawagan}}.

practice.q: “Ana bought a buko pie, and we ate it.”
options: {{Bumili si Ana ng buko pie, at kinain namin.}}
{{Binili si Ana ng buko pie, at kumain namin.}}
{{Bumili si Ana ng buko pie, at kumain kami ito.}}
practice.why: “A pie”: actor focus; “ate it” (that pie): object focus, {{kinain namin}}.

practice.tr: First I showered. Then I had breakfast.

practice.q: A friend asks about your weekend. Choose your replies.

lines.why: It's over: the completed form.

options: Lumangoy kami, tapos kumain kami ng inihaw na isda.
Lumalangoy kami, tapos kakain kami ng inihaw na isda.
lines.why: Finished things, one after another: completed forms.

practice.q: Say “Last week we went to Cebu.”
practice.answer: Noong isang linggo, pumunta kami sa Cebu.

practice.q: Your turn: tell what you did yesterday in three or four steps, with {{una}} and {{tapos}}, and at least one {{-in}}, {{i-}} or {{-an}} verb.

answers.t: Kahapon, nag-almusal muna ako. Tapos, tinawagan ko si Mama. Pagkatapos, pumunta ako sa mall at binili ko ang regalo ni Ben.
answers.tr: Yesterday I had breakfast first. Then I called Mom. After that, I went to the mall and bought Ben's present.

answers.t: Kagabi, nagluto ako ng adobo. Tapos, kinain namin ito habang nanonood ng TV.
answers.tr: Last night I cooked adobo. Then we ate it while watching TV.

lessons.title: Say you've just done something
lessons.summary: Say something has only just happened: “I've just eaten.” “She's just arrived.”
lessons.topic: The just-done form: {{ka-}} + the repeated syllable + the root ({{kakakain}}, {{kararating}}); the doer in the {{ko}} set; {{lang}}

dialog.t: Salamat po, pero kakakain ko lang.
dialog.tr: Thank you, but I've just eaten.

dialog.t: Kararating lang po niya. Gutom na po siya!

blocks.p: Tagalog has one more form, for something that has **just** happened: {{ka-}} + the root's first syllable repeated + the root, with no {{-um-}}, {{mag-}} or {{-in}}: {{kain}} → {{kakakain}} “have just eaten”, {{dating}} → {{kararating}} “have just arrived”.

table: {{Kagigising ko lang.}} I've just woken up.
{{Kaaalis lang ni Ben.}} Ben has just left.
{{Kauuwi ko lang.}} I've just got home.

blocks.p: **The doer is in the {{ko}} set**, whatever kind of verb it was: {{Kakakain ko lang}}, never {{ako}}. With a name, {{ni}}: {{Kaaalis lang ni Ben.}}
**Add {{lang}}** “just”: almost everyone does. It comes after {{ko}} and {{mo}}, but before {{niya}}, {{nila}} and names: {{Kakakain ko lang}}, {{Kararating lang niya}}.
In speech you'll often hear {{kaka-}} with every verb: {{kakarating}}, {{kakagising}}. Both are fine.

ex.t: Kauuwi lang namin galing sa Cebu.
ex.tr: We've just got back from Cebu.

ex.t: Kabibili ko lang ng cellphone na ito.

blocks.tip: This is the polite way to turn down food, which you will be offered a lot: {{Salamat po, kakakain ko lang.}}

mistakes.why: With this form, the doer is in the {{ko}} set.
{{Kumain lang ako}} means “I only ate”. For “I've just eaten”, use {{kakakain ko lang}}.

practice.why: The doer is in the {{ko}} set.
Just happened: {{ka-}} + {{ra}} + {{rating}}. ({{Dumating lang siya}} is “She only arrived”.)

practice.q: Ben's mom offers you food, but you've just eaten. You say…
practice.why: Polite, with {{po}}, and the just-done form.

practice.q: A friend calls you in the morning. Choose your replies.

lines.why: Just woke up: {{kagigising ko lang}}.
“Not yet”: {{hindi pa}} + the ongoing form.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you've just done today.

answers.t: Kagigising ko lang. Kakakain ko lang ng almusal.
answers.tr: I've just woken up. I've just had breakfast.

answers.t: Kauuwi ko lang galing sa trabaho. Kaliligo ko lang.
answers.tr: I've just got home from work. I've just showered.

lessons.title: Say what you've done, and never done
lessons.summary: Ask and answer “Have you ever…?”: “Have you ever been to Boracay?” “Not yet, but I've been to Palawan.”
lessons.topic: {{naka-}} / {{nakapag-}} + {{na}} for experience ({{nakapunta na}}); {{hindi pa}} + {{nakaka-}}; {{kahit minsan}}

goal.t: Nakapunta ka na ba sa Boracay?
goal.tr: Have you ever been to Boracay?

dialog.t: Nakapunta ka na ba sa Boracay?
dialog.tr: Have you ever been to Boracay?

dialog.t: Hindi pa. Pero nakapunta na ako sa Palawan.
dialog.tr: Not yet. But I've been to Palawan.

dialog.t: Nakakain ka na ba ng balut?
Hindi pa ako nakakakain ng balut! Masarap ba?
dialog.tr: I've never had balut! Is it good?

blocks.p: For experience, Tagalog uses {{naka-}} (on {{-um-}} roots) or {{nakapag-}} (on {{mag-}} roots), with {{na}} “already”: {{Nakapunta na ako sa Palawan.}} “I've been to Palawan.” {{Nakapag-aral ka na ba ng Espanyol?}} “Have you ever studied Spanish?”. The doer is in the {{ako}} set, and the thing takes {{ng}}: {{Nakakain ka na ba ng balut?}}

**Not yet, never**: {{hindi pa}} + the ongoing form, which repeats {{ka}} after {{naka-}}: {{Hindi pa ako nakakapunta sa Boracay.}} “I haven't been to Boracay (yet).” Stronger: {{kahit minsan}} “not even once”.
{{Hindi pa}} sounds hopeful: “not yet, but maybe one day”. That's how Filipinos usually answer; a flat “never” is rare.

ex.t: Nakapunta ka na ba sa Boracay?
ex.tr: Have you ever been to Boracay?

ex.t: Hindi pa ako nakakapunta sa Japan.
Nakasakay ka na ba ng jeep?
ex.tr: Have you ever ridden a jeepney?

ex.t: Nakakain na ako ng balut. Masarap pala!
ex.tr: I've had balut. It's actually good!

ex.t: Nakapag-aral ka na ba ng Espanyol?

blocks.tip: {{maka-}} also means “manage to, get to” (lesson 33): {{Nakapunta ka ba sa party?}} “Did you make it to the party?”. With {{na}} it's experience; without it, one time you managed.

mistakes.wrong: Pumunta ka na ba sa Boracay?
mistakes.right: Nakapunta ka na ba sa Boracay?
mistakes.tr: Have you ever been to Boracay?
mistakes.why: “Ever” is experience: {{naka-}}. {{Pumunta ka na ba?}} asks about one particular trip: “Have you gone yet?”

mistakes.wrong: Hindi pa ako nakapunta sa Japan.
mistakes.right: Hindi pa ako nakakapunta sa Japan.
mistakes.why: With {{hindi pa}}, the ongoing form: {{naka-}} + the repeated {{ka}}.

practice.tr: Have you ever been to Boracay?

practice.why: {{na}} comes right after the verb, before {{ako}}.

practice.tr: Have you ever ridden a jeepney?

practice.q: A Filipino friend asks about your travels. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Nakapunta ka na ba sa Cebu?
lines.tr: Have you ever been to Cebu?

options: Hindi pa, pero gusto kong pumunta!
Hindi na, pero gusto kong pumunta!
lines.why: Not yet: {{hindi pa}}. ({{hindi na}} is “not any more”.)

options: Oo, nakapunta na ako doon noong Disyembre.
Oo, pupunta na ako doon noong Disyembre.
lines.why: Done, last December: {{nakapunta na}}.

answers.t: Nakapunta na ako sa Maynila at sa Cebu. Hindi pa ako nakakasakay ng bangka, pero gusto ko!
answers.tr: I've been to Manila and Cebu. I've never been on a boat, but I'd like to!

lessons.title: Say what you saw, heard and understood
lessons.summary: Talk about seeing, hearing, understanding, knowing and remembering: “Have you seen Ana?” “Sorry, I didn't understand you.” “I don't know.”
lessons.topic: {{ma-}} object-focus verbs ({{makita}}, {{marinig}}, {{maintindihan}}, {{malaman}}, {{makalimutan}}); {{alam}} and {{kilala}}

dialog.t: Oo, nakita ko siya kanina sa canteen.
dialog.tr: Yes, I saw her earlier in the canteen.

dialog.t: Narinig mo ba ang balita? Ikakasal na siya!
dialog.tr: Did you hear the news? She's getting married!

dialog.t: Kilala mo ba ang boyfriend niya?
Hindi. Hindi ko pa siya nakikita.
dialog.tr: No. I haven't seen him yet.

blocks.p: Seeing, hearing and understanding just **happen** to you: you don't really choose to do them. Tagalog uses {{ma-}} for them, in **object focus**: the thing or person seen or heard takes {{ang}} or {{si}}, and the one who sees is in the {{ko}} set. {{Nakita ko si Ana.}} “I saw Ana.”

After {{hindi}}, the basic form means “can't”: {{Hindi ko maintindihan.}} “I can't understand it.” {{Hindi kita marinig.}} “I can't hear you.” The ongoing form is for now: {{Naiintindihan mo ba ako?}} “Do you understand me?”

**Know: two words.** {{alam}} is knowing a fact: {{Alam ko.}} “I know.”, {{Hindi ko alam.}} “I don't know.” {{kilala}} is knowing a person or a place: {{Kilala mo ba si Ben?}} “Do you know Ben?”. Neither changes for aspect, and the one who knows is in the {{ko}} set.
**Forgetting**: {{makalimutan}} “forget”: {{Nakalimutan ko!}} “I forgot!” And remembering: {{Naaalala mo pa ba ako?}} “Do you still remember me?”

blocks.tip: Two lifesavers for learners: {{Hindi ko po naintindihan. Pakiulit po.}} “I didn't understand. Could you say it again?” and {{Dahan-dahan lang po.}} “Slowly, please.”

mistakes.why: Object focus: the one who sees is {{ko}}; Ana, the one seen, takes {{si}}.
A person: {{kilala}}. {{alam}} is for facts.

mistakes.wrong: Hindi ko kilala kung nasaan siya.
mistakes.right: Hindi ko alam kung nasaan siya.
mistakes.tr: I don't know where she is.
mistakes.why: Where she is is a fact: {{alam}}.

practice.why: Object focus: the one who sees is {{mo}}.

practice.q: A vendor speaks too fast for you. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Isang daan at bente po lahat. May barya po ba kayo?
lines.tr: A hundred and twenty altogether. Do you have change?

options: Pasensya na po, hindi ko po naintindihan. Pakiulit po.
Pasensya na po, hindi ako naintindihan.
lines.why: {{hindi ko naintindihan}}: the one who didn't understand is {{ko}}.

options: Ah, naiintindihan ko na po. Heto po.
Ah, nakikita ko na po. Heto po.
lines.why: {{naiintindihan ko na}}: now I understand.

practice.q: Your turn: say something you saw or heard recently, and one thing you don't know.

answers.t: Nakita ko si Ben sa mall kahapon. Hindi ko alam kung saan siya nakatira.
answers.tr: I saw Ben at the mall yesterday. I don't know where he lives.

answers.t: Narinig ko ang balita kaninang umaga. Hindi ko alam kung totoo ito.
answers.tr: I heard the news this morning. I don't know if it's true.

lessons.title: Say what you can and can't do
lessons.summary: Say what you know how to do, what you can manage, and what you couldn't do this time: “Can you swim?” “I can do it!” “I couldn't sleep.”
lessons.topic: {{marunong}} “know how to”; {{kaya}} “can manage”; {{maka-}} / {{makapag-}} “be able to” ({{makatulog}}, {{makapunta}})

dialog.t: Oo, pero hindi ako makalangoy ngayon. Masakit ang paa ko.
dialog.tr: Yes, but I can't swim today. My foot hurts.

dialog.t: Ay, kawawa ka naman! Kaya mo bang maglakad?
dialog.tr: Oh, poor you! Can you walk?

dialog.t: Oo, kaya ko. Pero hindi ako nakatulog kagabi.
dialog.tr: Yes, I can manage. But I couldn't sleep last night.

blocks.p: English “can” is three different words in Tagalog, for three different meanings:

table: can manage, it's in my power

blocks.p: **{{marunong}}** “know how to”: the {{ako}} set with the linker, then the basic form: {{Marunong akong magluto.}} For languages, {{mag-}} + the language: {{Marunong ka bang mag-Tagalog?}} “Can you speak Tagalog?”
**{{kaya}}** “can (manage)”, with the {{ko}} set: {{Kaya ko!}} “I can do it!”, {{Hindi ko kaya.}} “I can't (manage it).”, {{Kaya mo bang maglakad?}} “Can you walk?”

**{{maka-}}** (on {{-um-}} roots) and **{{makapag-}}** (on {{mag-}} roots): being able to, on this occasion. The doer is in the {{ako}} set. Completed, {{naka-}} means “managed to”: {{Nakatulog ka ba?}} “Did you get any sleep?”, {{Hindi ako nakapunta.}} “I couldn't make it.” (With {{na}}, the same form tells experience: lesson 31.)

ex.tr: I know how to cook adobo.
I couldn't make it to the party.
Will you be able to come tomorrow?

blocks.tip: {{Kaya mo 'yan!}} “You can do it!” is how Filipinos cheer someone on.

mistakes.why: The pronoun is tied to the verb with the linker: {{akong}}.
{{kaya}} takes the {{ko}} set.
Not being able to this time: the {{maka-}} form of the verb.

practice.q: You couldn't make it to the party. You say…

lessons.title: Say how you feel
lessons.summary: Say you're hungry, sleepy, sad or happy, say what hurts, and react: “I'm exhausted.” “That's so funny!”
lessons.topic: Feelings as adjectives ({{gutom}}, {{pagod}}) and as verbs ({{inaantok}}, {{nalulungkot}}); {{pagod na pagod}}; {{masakit ang…}}; {{nakaka-}} “it makes one…”

goal.t: Inaantok na ako. Nakakapagod ang araw na ito.
goal.tr: I'm getting sleepy. Today has been so tiring.

dialog.t: Ano'ng nangyari sa iyo? Mukha kang pagod.
dialog.tr: What happened to you? You look tired.

dialog.t: Oo, pagod na pagod ako. Nakakapagod ang trabaho ngayon.
dialog.tr: Yes, I'm exhausted. Work was so tiring today.

dialog.t: Oo, nagugutom na ako. At masakit ang ulo ko.
dialog.tr: Yes, I'm getting hungry. And I have a headache.

dialog.t: Kawawa ka naman! Kain muna tayo.

blocks.p: **As describing words**, feelings come first like any adjective: {{Gutom ako.}} “I'm hungry.”, {{Pagod siya.}} “She's tired.”, {{Masaya kami.}} “We're happy.” Add {{na}} for “now”: {{Gutom na ako!}}

**As verbs**, for a feeling coming over you: {{-in}} verbs like {{inaantok}} “getting sleepy” and {{giniginaw}} “feeling cold”, and {{ma-}} verbs like {{nagugutom}} “getting hungry” and {{nalulungkot}} “feeling sad”. They're in the ongoing form, because the feeling is going on.
**Very**: say the describing word twice, with the linker: {{pagod na pagod}} “exhausted”, {{gutom na gutom}} “starving”, {{masayang masaya}} “really happy”.
**What hurts**: {{masakit}} “painful” + {{ang}} + the body part: {{Masakit ang ulo ko.}} “I have a headache.” {{Masakit ang tiyan ko.}} “My stomach hurts.” And {{May sakit ako.}} “I'm sick.”

**It makes me…**: {{nakaka-}} + a root says what something does to you: {{nakakapagod}} “tiring”, {{nakakatuwa}} “funny, delightful”, {{nakakatakot}} “scary”, {{nakakainis}} “annoying”, {{nakakahiya}} “embarrassing”. {{Nakakatakot ang pelikula!}} “The movie is scary!”

blocks.tip: {{Kawawa ka naman!}} “Poor you!” and {{Okay ka lang?}} “Are you okay?” are the caring answers when someone tells you how they feel.

mistakes.why: The feeling comes first, like any describing word.
{{nakakapagod}} is “tiring”, what something does to others: {{Nakakapagod ako}} would mean “I'm tiring”! You feel {{pagod}}.
The body part takes {{ang}}.

lessons.title: Say why
lessons.summary: Give reasons and results: “I couldn't go because it rained.” “It was raining, so we took a taxi.”
lessons.topic: {{kasi}}, {{dahil}} and {{dahil sa}} “because (of)”; {{kaya}} “so”; {{Bakit naman?}}

goal.tr: I couldn't go because it rained.

dialog.t: Bakit wala ka sa party kagabi?
dialog.tr: Why weren't you at the party last night?

dialog.t: Pasensya na, hindi ako nakapunta kasi may sakit ang anak ko.
dialog.tr: Sorry, I couldn't make it because my son was sick.

dialog.t: Ay, kawawa naman! Okay na ba siya?
dialog.tr: Oh, poor thing! Is he okay now?

dialog.t: Oo, okay na. Uminom siya ng gamot, kaya gumaling agad.
dialog.tr: Yes, he's fine now. He took some medicine, so he got better quickly.

blocks.p: **Because**: {{kasi}} is the everyday word; {{dahil}} is a little more careful, and the one you'll read. Both come before the reason: {{Hindi ako nakapunta kasi umulan.}} “I couldn't go because it rained.”
**Because of** + a noun: {{dahil sa}}: {{dahil sa ulan}} “because of the rain”, {{dahil sa traffic}}.

**So**: {{kaya}} brings in the result: {{Umuulan, kaya nag-taxi kami.}} “It was raining, so we took a taxi.” After {{kaya}} the pronoun may jump up or not: {{kaya ako umuwi}} and {{kaya umuwi ako}} are both said. ({{kaya}} is also “can manage”, lesson 33; the sentence tells you which.)

table: We took a taxi because it was raining.
It was raining, so we took a taxi.
I'm late because of the traffic.

blocks.p: **Asking why**: {{Bakit?}}. {{Bakit naman?}} is softer and more curious, “How come?”; {{Bakit hindi?}} “Why not?”. The pronoun jumps up after {{bakit}}: {{Bakit ka umiiyak?}} “Why are you crying?”

ex.tr: I couldn't go because it rained.
I'm late because of the traffic.
It was raining, so we took a taxi.

ex.t: Pagod ako, kaya maaga akong natulog.
ex.tr: I was tired, so I went to bed early.

ex.t: Nag-aaral ako ng Tagalog dahil gusto kong makausap ang pamilya ng asawa ko.
ex.tr: I'm learning Tagalog because I want to be able to talk to my wife's family.

blocks.tip: Starting an answer with {{kasi}} is how Filipinos explain themselves: {{Kasi… ang dami kong ginagawa.}} “It's just that… I've got so much to do.”

mistakes.tr: I couldn't go because it rained.
mistakes.why: {{kaya}} brings in a result (“so”), {{kasi}} a reason. The rain didn't happen because you stayed home!

mistakes.tr: I'm late because of the traffic.
mistakes.why: Before a noun on its own, “because of” is {{dahil sa}}.

lessons.title: Say when, and in what order
lessons.summary: Join two actions in time: “Before you eat, wash your hands.” “While Mom was cooking, we played.” “When I was a kid…”
lessons.topic: {{bago}} “before”, {{pagkatapos}} “after”, {{habang}} “while”, {{kapag}} / {{pag}} “when, whenever”, {{noong}} “when (in the past)”, and the verb form after each

goal.t: Bago kumain, maghugas ka ng kamay.
goal.tr: Before you eat, wash your hands.

dialog.t: Bago kumain, maghugas kayo ng kamay!
dialog.tr: Before you eat, wash your hands!

dialog.t: Opo! Pagkatapos naming kumain, pwede po ba kaming maglaro?
dialog.tr: Okay! After we eat, can we play?

dialog.t: Sige, pero kapag dumilim na, umuwi kayo agad.
dialog.tr: All right, but when it gets dark, come home right away.

blocks.p: **{{bago}} “before”** + the basic form: {{Bago kumain, maghugas ka ng kamay.}} To say who, the pronoun comes right after {{bago}}: {{Bago ka umalis, tawagan mo ako.}} “Before you leave, call me.”

**{{pagkatapos}} “after”** + a noun with {{ng}} ({{pagkatapos ng trabaho}} “after work”), or + the {{ko}} set, the linker and the basic form: {{Pagkatapos kong kumain, natulog ako.}} “After I ate, I took a nap.”
**{{habang}} “while”** + the ongoing form: {{Habang nagluluto si Nanay, naglalaro kami.}} “While Mom was cooking, we played.”

**{{kapag}} (in speech {{pag}}) “when, whenever”**: for what happens every time, with the ongoing form ({{Kapag umuulan, nasa bahay lang ako.}} “When it rains, I just stay home.”), and for a moment still to come, with the completed form: {{Kapag dumating siya, tawagan mo ako.}} “When she gets here, call me.”
**{{noong}} “when (in the past)”**: {{Noong dumating siya, kumakain kami.}} “When she arrived, we were eating.” {{Noong bata pa ako…}} “When I was a kid…” needs no verb at all.

ex.t: Bago kumain, maghugas ka ng kamay.
ex.tr: Before you eat, wash your hands.

ex.t: Bago ka umalis, tawagan mo ako.

ex.tr: After I ate, I took a nap.

ex.t: Habang nagluluto si Nanay, naglalaro kami.
ex.tr: While Mom was cooking, we played.

ex.t: Kapag umuulan, nasa bahay lang ako.
ex.tr: When it rains, I just stay home.

ex.t: Pag dumating siya, tawagan mo ako.
ex.tr: When she gets here, call me.

ex.t: Noong bata pa ako, nakatira kami sa Batangas.
ex.tr: When I was a kid, we lived in Batangas.

blocks.tip: {{kapag}} looks ahead, or is about every time; {{noong}} looks back at one time. {{Kapag pumunta ka sa Cebu…}} “When you go to Cebu (one day)…”, but {{Noong pumunta ako sa Cebu…}} “When I went to Cebu…”.

mistakes.right: Bago kumain, maghugas ka ng kamay.
mistakes.tr: Before you eat, wash your hands.
mistakes.why: After {{bago}}, the basic form.

mistakes.wrong: Habang nagluto si Nanay, naglalaro kami.
mistakes.right: Habang nagluluto si Nanay, naglalaro kami.

mistakes.right: Noong bata pa ako, nakatira kami sa Batangas.
mistakes.tr: When I was a kid, we lived in Batangas.
mistakes.why: Looking back at the past: {{noong}}.

lessons.title: Compare people and things
lessons.summary: Say which is bigger, which is the best, or that two are the same: “Manila is bigger than Cebu.” “Grandma's adobo is the best!”
lessons.topic: {{mas}} … {{kaysa (sa)}}; {{pinaka-}}; {{kasing-}} and {{magkasing-}}; {{alin}} “which”; {{mas gusto}} “prefer”

dialog.t: Alin ang mas maganda, Boracay o Palawan?
dialog.tr: Which is nicer, Boracay or Palawan?

dialog.t: Para sa akin, mas maganda ang Palawan. Mas tahimik doon kaysa sa Boracay.
dialog.tr: For me, Palawan is nicer. It's quieter there than in Boracay.

dialog.t: Pareho silang masarap! Pero ang pinakamasarap na pagkain, nasa bahay ni Lola!
dialog.tr: They're both delicious! But the best food is at Grandma's house!

blocks.p: **More, -er**: {{mas}} + the adjective: {{mas malaki}} “bigger”, {{mas mura}} “cheaper”. The adjective still comes first in the sentence: {{Mas malaki ang Maynila.}} “Manila is bigger.”
**Than**: {{kaysa sa}} (with a name, {{kaysa kay}}): {{Mas malaki ang Maynila kaysa sa Cebu.}} “Manila is bigger than Cebu.” {{Mas matangkad si Ben kaysa kay Mark.}} “Ben is taller than Mark.”

**The most, -est**: {{pinaka-}} joined to the adjective: {{pinakamalaki}} “the biggest”, {{pinakamasarap}} “the most delicious, the best”. With a noun, add the linker: {{ang pinakamagandang beach}} “the most beautiful beach”.

**As … as**: {{kasing-}} + the root, without {{ma-}}: {{Kasingtaas ni Ben si Mark.}} “Mark is as tall as Ben.” For two together, {{magkasing-}}: {{Magkasingtaas sila.}} “They're the same height.” And simply {{pareho}} “both, the same”: {{Pareho silang masarap.}} “They're both delicious.”
**Which?** {{alin}}, for choosing between things: {{Alin ang mas mura?}} “Which one is cheaper?”

ex.t: Mas malaki ang Maynila kaysa sa Cebu.
Mas matangkad si Ben kaysa kay Mark.
Ito ang pinakamagandang beach sa Pilipinas.
ex.tr: This is the most beautiful beach in the Philippines.
My brother and I are the same height.

ex.t: Mas gusto ko ang kape kaysa sa tsaa.
ex.tr: I like coffee better than tea.

blocks.tip: {{mas gusto}} is the everyday “prefer, would rather”: {{Mas gusto kong manood sa bahay.}} “I'd rather watch at home.”

mistakes.why: After {{kaysa}}, a name takes {{kay}}.

lessons.title: Sound natural with the little words
lessons.summary: Use the little words that give Tagalog its warmth (“just”, “oh, so…”, “I think”, “first”, “too”) and put them in the right order.
lessons.topic: The particles {{lang}}, {{naman}}, {{nga}}, {{pala}}, {{muna}}, {{yata}}, {{din}} / {{rin}}, {{daw}} / {{raw}}; their place and their order

goal.t: Ikaw pala si Ben! Kumusta ka naman?
goal.tr: Oh, so you're Ben! And how are you?

dialog.tr: Oh, so you're Ben! How are you?

dialog.t: Mabuti naman. Ikaw si Ana, di ba?
Oo! Kumain ka na ba? Kain muna tayo.
dialog.tr: Yes! Have you eaten? Let's eat first.

dialog.t: Sige, pero kaunti lang. Busog pa yata ako.
dialog.tr: Okay, but just a little. I think I'm still full.

dialog.t: Ako rin! Kape na lang tayo.
dialog.tr: Me too! Let's just have coffee.

blocks.p: Tagalog has a set of little words that add a feeling to a sentence: “just”, “really”, “oh, so…”, “I think”, “first”. They're why two sentences with the same words can sound cold or warm. You've met {{po}}, {{ba}}, {{na}} and {{pa}}; here are the others.

blocks.means: a little word that doesn't name anything but adds a feeling or a shade of meaning: {{po}}, {{ba}}, {{na}}, {{lang}}, {{naman}}.

table: just, only; makes things smaller and softer
{{Mabuti naman.}} I'm fine. {{Ikaw naman?}} And you?
{{Oo nga!}} That's right! {{Pakiabot nga.}} Could you pass it?
{{Ikaw pala si Ben!}} Oh, so you're Ben!
{{Uulan yata.}} I think it's going to rain.
{{Masarap daw dito.}} They say it's good here.

blocks.p: **Where they go**: like {{ba}}, right after the first word or phrase: {{Busog pa yata ako.}} After {{hindi}}, they come right after it: {{Hindi naman ako galit.}} “I'm not angry, really.”

**Their order**, when several meet: first the short pronouns {{ka}}, {{ko}}, {{mo}}; then {{na}} or {{pa}}; then the other little words ({{lang}}, {{din}}, {{po}}, {{ba}}…); last, the longer pronouns like {{ako}}, {{siya}}, {{kayo}}. {{Kumain ka na ba?}}, {{Kumain na po ba kayo?}}, {{Busog pa yata ako.}}

**{{din}} or {{rin}}, {{daw}} or {{raw}}**: after a vowel (or w, y) say {{rin}} and {{raw}}; after a consonant, {{din}} and {{daw}}. {{Ako rin.}} {{Pagod din ako.}} {{Uuwi raw siya.}} {{Masarap daw.}}

ex.tr: I think it's going to rain later.
They say the food here is good.

blocks.tip: {{di ba?}} at the end of a sentence is “right?”: {{Taga-Cebu ka, di ba?}} “You're from Cebu, right?”. You'll hear it all the time.

mistakes.why: After a vowel, {{din}} becomes {{rin}}.
The little word comes before a longer pronoun like {{tayo}}.
{{pa}} comes right after the first word, before {{ako}}.

lessons.title: Say which one: “the woman who…”, “the book I bought”
lessons.summary: Point people and things out by what they did or what was done to them: “the woman who lives next door”, “the phone I bought yesterday”.
lessons.topic: Clauses tied on with the linker: {{ang babaeng nakatira sa tabi namin}}, {{ang cellphone na binili ko}}; the focus decides who is meant

goal.t: Siya ang babaeng nakatira sa tabi namin.
goal.tr: She's the woman who lives next door to us.

dialog.t: Sino iyong lalaking kausap ni Ana?
dialog.tr: Who's that man Ana's talking to?

dialog.t: Siya ang gurong nagturo sa akin ng Ingles.
dialog.tr: He's the teacher who taught me English.

dialog.t: Ah! E iyong babaeng nakasuot ng pula?
dialog.tr: Oh! And the woman in red?

dialog.t: Asawa niya iyon. Siya ang nagluto ng pansit na kinain natin!
dialog.tr: That's his wife. She's the one who cooked the pancit we ate!

blocks.p: To say **which** person or thing you mean, Tagalog ties a whole description to the noun with the linker, just like an adjective (lesson 9): {{ang babaeng nakatira sa tabi namin}} “the woman who lives next to us”, word for word “the woman-that living next to us”. No separate word for “who” or “which” is needed.

blocks.means: a group of words with its own verb inside a bigger sentence: “who lives next door”, “that I bought”.

blocks.p: **The focus decides who is meant.** The noun is always the one **in focus** of the verb in the clause. With an actor-focus verb, the noun is the doer: {{ang taong bumili ng bahay}} “the person who bought a house”. With an object-focus verb, the noun is the thing: {{ang bahay na binili ni Ben}} “the house Ben bought”.

table: the child who ate the cake

blocks.p: So {{ang batang kumain}} is the child who ate, and {{ang kinain ng bata}} is what the child ate. Mix up the focus and you change who did what.
**Without the noun**, {{ang}} + the verb means “the one who…, what…”: {{Siya ang nagluto.}} “She's the one who cooked.” (lesson 27), {{Ito ang binili ko.}} “This is what I bought.”

ex.t: Siya ang babaeng nakatira sa tabi namin.
ex.tr: She's the woman who lives next door.

ex.t: Nasaan ang cellphone na binili ko kahapon?
ex.tr: Where's the phone I bought yesterday?

ex.t: Kilala mo ba ang lalaking kausap ni Ana?

ex.t: Masarap ang pansit na niluto ni Lola.
ex.tr: The pancit Grandma cooked is delicious.

ex.t: Mababait ang mga taong nagtatrabaho dito.
ex.tr: The people who work here are nice.

ex.t: Ito ang lugar na pinuntahan namin noong bakasyon.
ex.tr: This is the place we went to on vacation.

blocks.tip: {{iyong}} ({{iyon}} + the linker), in speech {{yung}}, is how people say “that one…, you know, the…”: {{Yung babaeng nakapula, sino siya?}} “That woman in red, who is she?”

lessons.title: Pass on what someone said
lessons.summary: Report what you heard and what people asked: “Ana says she'll come later.” “He asked if we can wait.”
lessons.topic: {{daw}} / {{raw}}; {{sabi ni…}}, {{sinabi niya na…}}; {{tinanong niya kung…}} “asked whether”

goal.t: Sabi ni Ana, pupunta raw siya mamaya.

dialog.t: Male-late daw siya kasi traffic sa EDSA. Tinanong niya kung pwede tayong maghintay.
dialog.tr: She says she'll be late because there's traffic on EDSA. She asked if we can wait.

dialog.t: Sige. Sabihin mo sa kanya na hihintayin natin siya.
dialog.tr: Okay. Tell her we'll wait for her.

blocks.p: **{{daw}} / {{raw}} “he says, she says, they say”** is the quickest way to pass something on. Keep the sentence as it was said, change the pronoun to fit (as in English), and slip {{daw}} in after the first word: {{Pagod ako.}} “I'm tired.” → {{Pagod daw siya.}} “She says she's tired.” After a vowel it's {{raw}}: {{Uuwi raw siya.}} “She says she's coming home.” It also means “I've heard, people say”: {{Uulan daw bukas.}} “They say it'll rain tomorrow.”
**{{sabi ni…}} “… says, … said”** names who said it, usually at the start: {{Sabi ni Ana, pupunta raw siya.}} Filipinos often keep {{daw}} as well. With a noun: {{Sabi ng doktor…}} “The doctor says…”

**{{sinabi niya na…}} “she said that…”**: the full verb {{sabihin}} (object focus), with {{na}} “that” before the words said: {{Sinabi niya na pagod siya.}} “He said he was tired.” As a command: {{Sabihin mo sa kanya na…}} “Tell her that…”

**Questions**: {{tinanong niya kung…}} “she asked if…”: {{Tinanong niya kung pwede tayong maghintay.}} With a question word, keep the question word: {{Tinanong niya kung saan ka nakatira.}} “She asked where you live.”

table: {{Pagod daw siya.}} / {{Sinabi niya na pagod siya.}}

blocks.p: Unlike English (“she said she **was** tired”), Tagalog keeps the verb form the speaker used: {{Sinabi niya na pagod siya.}}, {{Pupunta raw siya.}}

ex.t: Sabi ni Ana, pupunta raw siya mamaya.

ex.t: Tinanong niya kung libre ka sa Sabado.
ex.tr: He asked if you're free on Saturday.

ex.t: Sabihin mo sa kanya na tatawag ako mamaya.

blocks.tip: {{daw}} also passes on instructions: {{Kumain ka na raw.}} “(Mom) says you should eat now.” Filipinos like it because it says “these aren't my words”: a gentle way to deliver news or orders.

mistakes.why: Change the pronoun to fit who's talking: she said it about herself, so {{siya}}.
A yes-or-no question passed on: “whether, if” is {{kung}}, not {{na}}.

lessons.title: Say what you think
lessons.summary: Give your opinion, agree and disagree gently: “I think the red one is nicer.” “You're right.” “I thought it was cheap!”
lessons.topic: {{sa tingin ko}}, {{sa palagay ko}}, {{para sa akin}}; {{akala ko}} “I thought (but no)”; {{mukhang}} “it looks”; agreeing and disagreeing

goal.t: Sa tingin ko, mas maganda ang pula.
goal.tr: I think the red one is nicer.

dialog.t: Ano sa tingin mo, alin ang mas maganda?
dialog.tr: What do you think, which one is nicer?

dialog.t: Sa tingin ko, mas maganda ang pula. Pero mukhang mahal.
dialog.tr: I think the red one is nicer. But it looks expensive.

dialog.t: Akala ko mura lang! Tatlong libo pala.
dialog.tr: I thought it was cheap! Turns out it's three thousand.

dialog.t: Ang mahal! Para sa akin, hindi sulit.
dialog.tr: So expensive! For me, it's not worth it.

dialog.t: Sang-ayon ako. Tingnan natin ang iba.
dialog.tr: I agree. Let's look at the others.

blocks.p: **I think**: {{sa tingin ko}} (word for word “in my view”) or {{sa palagay ko}}, at the start, often with a comma: {{Sa tingin ko, uulan mamaya.}} “I think it'll rain later.” Asking: {{Ano sa tingin mo?}} “What do you think?”
**For me**: {{para sa akin}} “for me, in my opinion”: {{Para sa akin, mas masarap ang adobo.}}

**I thought (but I was wrong)**: {{akala ko}}: {{Akala ko sarado ang tindahan.}} “I thought the store was closed (but it isn't).” It usually means you've found out otherwise, often with {{pala}}: {{Akala ko mura. Mahal pala!}} For what you think now, use {{sa tingin ko}}.
**It looks…**: {{mukhang}} ({{mukha}} “face, look” + the linker), then an adjective or a whole sentence: {{Mukhang masarap!}} “It looks delicious!” {{Mukhang uulan.}} “It looks like rain.”

**Agreeing**: {{Sang-ayon ako.}} “I agree.”, {{Tama ka.}} “You're right.”, {{Oo nga.}} “That's true.” **Disagreeing**: {{Hindi ako sang-ayon.}} “I don't agree.” Filipinos usually soften a no with {{parang}} “it seems, kind of” or {{siguro}} “maybe”: {{Parang hindi.}} “I don't think so.”

table: I don't agree. I don't think so.

ex.tr: I think it's going to rain later.

ex.t: Para sa akin, mas masarap ang adobo.

ex.tr: I thought the store was closed.

blocks.tip: {{Ewan ko}} “I dunno” (more offhand than {{Hindi ko alam}}) and {{Bahala na}} “Whatever happens, happens” are two very Filipino ways of not giving a firm answer.

mistakes.right: Sa tingin ko, maganda ang Palawan.
mistakes.why: {{akala ko}} means you thought so but were wrong. For your opinion now: {{sa tingin ko}}.
{{mukha}} is tied to what follows with the linker: {{mukhang}}.
{{sa tingin ko}} is “in my view”: the {{ko}} set.

lessons.title: Talk about what will happen if…
lessons.summary: Talk about conditions and give advice: “If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.” “If I were you, I'd take a taxi.”
lessons.topic: {{kung}} and {{kapag}} + a condition, the not-yet-begun form in the result; {{kung ako sa iyo}}; imagining with {{kung}}

goal.t: Kung umulan bukas, hindi tayo tutuloy.
goal.tr: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.

dialog.t: Tuloy ba tayo sa beach bukas?
dialog.tr: Are we still on for the beach tomorrow?

dialog.t: Oo, pero kung umulan, hindi tayo tutuloy.
dialog.tr: Yes, but if it rains, we won't go.

dialog.t: Kung hindi tayo tutuloy, ano ang gagawin natin?
dialog.tr: If we don't go, what will we do?

dialog.t: Manonood na lang tayo ng sine.
Sige! Kung ako sa iyo, magdadala ako ng payong.
dialog.tr: Okay! If I were you, I'd bring an umbrella.

blocks.p: **If**: {{kung}} + the condition, then the result: {{Kung umulan bukas, hindi tayo tutuloy.}} “If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.” The result hasn't happened, so it's in the **not-yet-begun** form ({{tutuloy}}, {{manonood}}).

**The condition**: for an event, you'll usually hear the completed form, as if picturing it done ({{kung umulan}} “if it rains”, {{kung dumating siya}} “if she comes”); the not-yet-begun form ({{kung uulan}}) is heard too. For a state, just the adjective or {{may}}: {{Kung pagod ka…}} “If you're tired…”, {{Kung may oras ka…}} “If you have time…”

**{{kung}} or {{kapag}}?** {{kapag}} is for something you expect (“when”), {{kung}} for something that may or may not happen (“if”): {{Kapag dumating si Ben, kakain na tayo.}} “When Ben gets here, we'll eat.” {{Kung dumating si Ben, kakain tayo.}} “If Ben comes, we'll eat.”
**Advice**: {{Kung ako sa iyo,…}} “If I were you,…”, word for word “if I (were) in your place”: {{Kung ako sa iyo, mag-ta-taxi ako.}} “If I were you, I'd take a taxi.”

**Imagining**: Tagalog uses the same pattern for things that aren't true: {{Kung mayaman ako, bibili ako ng bahay sa Boracay.}} “If I were rich, I'd buy a house in Boracay.” The verb doesn't change; the situation tells you it's imagined. (Lesson 43 adds {{sana}} for wishes and regrets.)

ex.t: Kung umulan bukas, hindi tayo tutuloy.
ex.tr: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.

ex.t: Kung may oras ka, tawagan mo ako.
ex.tr: If you have time, call me.

ex.t: Kapag dumating si Ben, kakain na tayo.
ex.tr: When Ben gets here, we'll eat.

ex.t: Kung pagod ka, magpahinga ka muna.

ex.tr: If I were you, I'd take a taxi.

ex.t: Kung mayaman ako, bibili ako ng bahay sa Boracay.
ex.tr: If I were rich, I'd buy a house in Boracay.

ex.t: Hindi ako sasama kung hindi ka sasama.
ex.tr: I won't go if you don't.

blocks.tip: {{kung}} has three jobs, all a kind of “if”: “if” ({{kung umulan}}), “whether” ({{Tinanong niya kung…}}, lesson 40), and, with a question word, an indirect question ({{Hindi ko alam kung saan siya nakatira.}} “I don't know where she lives.”).

lessons.title: Wish, hope and regret
lessons.summary: Say what you hope for and what you wish had happened: “I hope you can come.” “I should have studied.” “What a shame!”
lessons.topic: {{sana}} for hopes and wishes; {{sana}} + the completed form for regrets; {{Sayang!}}

goal.t: Sana makapunta ka sa birthday ko!
goal.tr: I hope you can come to my birthday!

dialog.t: Sana makapunta ka sa birthday ko sa Sabado!
dialog.tr: I hope you can make it to my birthday on Saturday!

dialog.t: Sana nga! Pero may trabaho ako. Sayang!
dialog.tr: I hope so! But I have work. What a shame!

dialog.t: Ay, sayang naman! Noong isang taon, hindi ka rin nakapunta.
dialog.tr: Oh, too bad! Last year you couldn't come either.
Right. I should have taken the day off.

dialog.t: Sige, sa susunod na taon na lang!

blocks.p: **Hoping**: {{sana}} “I hope, hopefully” comes first, then the sentence: {{Sana umaraw bukas.}} “I hope it's sunny tomorrow.” With being able: {{Sana makapunta ka.}} “I hope you can come.”
**Wishing things were different now**: {{sana}} + what you wish: {{Sana nandito ka.}} “I wish you were here.” {{Sana mayaman ako.}} “I wish I were rich.”

**Regret, “should have”**: {{sana}} + the **completed** form: {{Sana nag-aral ako.}} “I should have studied.” With {{hindi}}: {{Sana hindi ako kumain nang marami.}} “I shouldn't have eaten so much.” With {{mag-}} verbs you can hear the difference: {{Sana mag-aral ka}} “I hope you'll study”, but {{Sana nag-aral ka}} “You should have studied”. With {{-um-}} verbs the two look alike ({{Sana pumunta ka}}), and the situation tells you which.

table: I shouldn't have eaten so much.

blocks.p: **What a shame!** {{Sayang!}} “Too bad! What a waste!”: {{Sayang, hindi ka nakapunta!}} “Too bad you couldn't come!” It's also for wasted things: {{Sayang ang pagkain.}} “That food is going to waste.”

ex.t: Sana makapunta ka sa birthday ko.
ex.tr: I hope you can come to my birthday.

ex.t: Sana hindi ako kumain nang marami.
ex.tr: I shouldn't have eaten so much.
Too bad you couldn't make it!

blocks.tip: {{Sana all!}} (“I wish everyone had that!”) is what Filipinos say, half joking, when a friend shows off a new phone, a trip or a sweet boyfriend.

mistakes.why: A hope about tomorrow: the basic form. {{nag-aral}} after {{sana}} is a regret about the past.
The pronoun goes after the verb here: {{makapunta ka}}.

{{Sana nga!}} “I really hope so!”

lessons.title: Have something done, and make someone do it
lessons.summary: Say you had something done (“I got a haircut”) and that someone made or let someone do something (“Mom made me clean my room”).
lessons.topic: The causative: {{magpa-}} “have it done” ({{nagpagupit}}), {{ipa-}} for the thing ({{ipaayos}}), {{pa-…-in}} “make or let someone” ({{pinakain}}, {{pinaglinis}})

dialog.t: Oo, kahapon. Pinapunta ako ni Mama sa barbero.
dialog.tr: Yes, yesterday. Mom sent me to the barber.

dialog.t: May kasal kasi ang pinsan ko. Pinaglinis din niya ako ng sapatos!
dialog.tr: My cousin's getting married. She made me clean my shoes too!

dialog.t: Ipaayos mo na rin ang relo mo. Sira na iyan!
dialog.tr: Get your watch fixed too. It's broken!

blocks.means: a verb for causing an action: having it done, or making or letting someone do it. In Tagalog it has {{pa-}} in it.

blocks.p: **Having something done for you**: {{magpa-}} + the root: {{gupit}} “cut” → {{magpagupit}} “get a haircut”, {{ayos}} “fix” → {{magpaayos}} “have something fixed”, {{masahe}} → {{magpamasahe}} “get a massage”. It's actor focus, so you're {{ako}}: {{Nagpagupit ako.}} “I got a haircut.”
**The thing you have done, in focus**: {{ipa-}} + the root: {{Ipaayos mo ang relo mo.}} “Get your watch fixed.” {{Ipinaayos ko na.}} “I've already had it fixed.”

**Making or letting someone do it**: {{pa-…-in}}, with the person made to do it in focus: {{pakainin}} “feed” (make eat), {{papuntahin}} “send” (make go). Completed: {{pinakain}}, {{pinapunta}}. For {{mag-}} verbs, {{pag-…-in}}: {{paglinisin}} “make (someone) clean” → {{pinaglinis}}. {{Pinaglinis ako ni Nanay ng kuwarto.}} “Mom made me clean my room.” The one who causes it takes {{ni}} / {{ng}} or the {{ko}} set.
“Make” or “let”? The situation tells you: {{Pinauwi kami nang maaga.}} “They let us go home early” (or “sent us home early”).

ex.tr: I'm getting my phone fixed tomorrow.

ex.t: Pinaglinis ako ni Nanay ng kuwarto.
ex.tr: Mom made me clean my room.

ex.t: Pinapunta ako ng boss ko sa Cebu.
ex.tr: My boss sent me to Cebu.
They let us go home early.

blocks.tip: A good Filipino host tells the kids: {{Papasukin mo siya.}} “Let him in.” and {{Paupuin mo ang bisita.}} “Have the guest sit down.”

lessons.title: Say something happened by accident
lessons.summary: Say you broke, dropped, spilled or forgot something without meaning to: “Sorry, I broke the glass.” “I left my umbrella on the jeepney.”
lessons.topic: {{ma-}} for accidents ({{nabasag}}, {{natapon}}, {{naiwan}}, {{nawala}}); {{na-}} for things that happen to you ({{nadulas}}, {{naligaw}})

dialog.t: Sorry po, nabasag ko ang baso.

dialog.tr: That's all right, dear. Did it fall?

dialog.t: Opo, nadulas po sa kamay ko.
dialog.tr: Yes, it slipped out of my hand.
As long as you didn't get hurt.

blocks.p: Tagalog shows whether you **meant** to do something. {{Binasag ko ang baso}} says you broke the glass on purpose; {{Nabasag ko ang baso}} says it broke while you had it, by accident. The {{ma-}} form (completed {{na-}}) means “it happened; nobody planned it”.

**With no one to blame**, leave the doer out and the thing stays in focus: {{Nabasag ang baso.}} “The glass broke.” {{Nahulog ang cellphone ko.}} “My phone fell.” {{Nawala ang susi ko.}} “My key got lost.”

**Things that happen to you**: the same {{na-}} for little misfortunes, with you in focus: {{nadulas}} “slipped”, {{nasugatan}} “got hurt”, {{naligaw}} “got lost”, {{nabasa}} “got wet”. The Taglish {{na-late}} and {{na-traffic}} (lesson 28) work the same way.

**Apologizing**: {{Sorry}} or {{Pasensya na}} + what happened: {{Pasensya na, naiwan ko ang payong mo.}} “Sorry, I left your umbrella somewhere.” And to reassure someone: {{Okay lang.}} “It's okay.”, {{Hindi bale.}} “Never mind.”

ex.t: Nahulog ang cellphone ko sa tubig!
ex.tr: My phone fell in the water!

ex.t: Naiwan ko ang payong ko sa jeep.
ex.tr: I left my umbrella on the jeepney.

ex.t: Natapon ko ang kape sa damit ko.
ex.tr: I spilled coffee on my clothes.

ex.note: word for word “my key got lost”

blocks.tip: Filipinos usually say {{Nawala}} “it got lost” rather than “I lost it”: the {{na-}} form is a gentle way to talk about mistakes, yours and other people's.

mistakes.wrong: Binasag ko ang baso. Sorry, hindi sinasadya.
mistakes.right: Nabasag ko ang baso. Sorry, hindi sinasadya.
mistakes.tr: I broke the glass. Sorry, I didn't mean to.
mistakes.why: {{binasag}} says you broke it on purpose. By accident: {{nabasag}}.
The umbrella is in focus; the one it happened to is in the {{ko}} set.

practice.tr: Sorry, I broke the glass (by accident).

lessons.title: Say how things used to be
lessons.summary: Talk about how life was and what you used to do: “When I was a kid, we always played in the street.” “I don't smoke any more.”
lessons.topic: {{dati}}, {{noon}}, {{noong bata pa ako}} + the ongoing form for past habits; {{hindi na}} “not any more”; {{dating}} “former”

goal.t: Noong bata pa ako, lagi kaming naglalaro sa kalye.
goal.tr: When I was a kid, we always used to play in the street.

dialog.t: Lola, ano po ang ginagawa ninyo noong bata pa kayo?
dialog.tr: Grandma, what did you do when you were little?

dialog.t: Noon, wala pang cellphone. Naglalaro kami ng tumbang preso sa labas.
dialog.tr: Back then there were no cell phones yet. We used to play tumbang preso outside.

dialog.t: Naglalakad kami papunta sa eskuwela, isang oras araw-araw!
dialog.tr: We used to walk to school, an hour every day!

dialog.t: Oo. Dati, mas simple ang buhay.
dialog.tr: Yes. Life used to be simpler.

blocks.p: **What used to happen**, again and again, takes the **ongoing** form, with a past time word to set the scene: {{dati}} “before, in the past”, {{noon}} “back then”, {{noong bata pa ako}} “when I was a kid”. The ongoing form says it went on and on; the time word says it's over.
Compare: {{Naglaro kami sa labas.}} “We played outside (that time).” and {{Naglalaro kami sa labas noon.}} “We used to play outside.”

table: {{Naglalaro kami noon.}} We used to play.
{{Naglalakad kami dati.}} We used to walk.
{{Tumira kami sa Cebu.}} We lived in Cebu (for a time).
{{Nakatira kami dati sa Cebu.}} We used to live in Cebu.

blocks.p: **Not any more**: {{hindi na}} + the ongoing form: {{Hindi na ako naninigarilyo.}} “I don't smoke any more.” For things, {{wala na}}: {{Wala na ang lumang bahay namin.}} “Our old house isn't there any more.”
**Former**: {{dating}} ({{dati}} + the linker) before a noun: {{ang dating bahay namin}} “our old house”, {{ang dating guro ko}} “my former teacher”.

ex.t: Noong bata pa ako, lagi kaming naglalaro sa kalye.
ex.tr: When I was a kid, we always used to play in the street.
We used to live in the province.

ex.t: Naglalakad kami papunta sa eskuwela noon.
ex.tr: Back then we used to walk to school.
Back then there were no cell phones yet.

blocks.tip: Older Filipinos love to talk about {{noong araw}} “the old days”: many of their stories start {{Noong araw…}}

mistakes.wrong: Noong bata pa ako, naglaro kami sa labas araw-araw.

mistakes.why: Again and again in the past (“used to”): the ongoing form. The completed form is for one time.

lessons.title: Tell a story
lessons.summary: Tell a real story from beginning to end: set the scene, say what happened, and how it ended.
lessons.topic: The ongoing form for the scene ({{habang naglalakad ako}}), the completed form for events; {{isang araw}}, {{bigla}}, {{hanggang}}, {{sa wakas}}

goal.t: Habang naglalakad ako pauwi, biglang umulan nang malakas.
goal.tr: As I was walking home, it suddenly started pouring.

dialog.t: Alam mo ba ang nangyari sa akin kahapon?
dialog.tr: Do you know what happened to me yesterday?

dialog.t: Habang naglalakad ako pauwi, biglang umulan nang malakas. Wala akong payong!
dialog.tr: As I was walking home, it suddenly started pouring. I didn't have an umbrella!

dialog.t: Sumilong ako sa isang tindahan. Doon, nakita ko si Mark, ang dati kong kaklase!
dialog.tr: I took shelter in a shop. And there I saw Mark, my old classmate!

dialog.t: Oo! Nagkuwentuhan kami hanggang tumigil ang ulan. Sa wakas, nakauwi rin ako.
dialog.tr: Yes! We chatted until the rain stopped. Finally I made it home.

blocks.p: A good story uses two forms side by side. The **ongoing** form sets the scene, what was going on: {{Habang naglalakad ako pauwi,…}} “As I was walking home,…”. The **completed** form tells the events, one after another: {{…biglang umulan.}} “…it suddenly rained.”
{{bigla}} “suddenly” is tied to the verb with the linker: {{biglang umulan}}, {{biglang dumating si Ben}}.

**Everything together**: object focus for a particular person or thing ({{nakita ko si Mark}}), {{maka-}} for what you managed ({{nakauwi rin ako}}), {{na-}} for accidents ({{nabasa ako}} “I got wet”). Storytellers pull the listener in with {{Alam mo ba?}} “You know what?”, and listeners keep it going with {{Tapos?}}, {{Talaga?}}, {{Grabe!}} “No way!”.

ex.t: Isang araw, nawala ang aso namin.
ex.tr: One day our dog went missing.

ex.t: Habang nagluluto si Nanay, biglang namatay ang ilaw.
ex.tr: While Mom was cooking, the lights suddenly went out.

ex.t: Hinanap namin siya sa buong barangay.
ex.tr: We looked for him all over the neighborhood.

ex.t: Wala kaming nakita, kaya umuwi kami.
ex.tr: We didn't find anything, so we went home.

ex.t: Sa wakas, bumalik siya, gutom na gutom!

blocks.tip: Filipinos tell stories with a lot of {{tapos}}: {{tapos… tapos… tapos…}}. Using it in every sentence is perfectly normal; that's what it's for.

lessons.title: Keep a conversation going
lessons.summary: React, ask follow-up questions and turn questions back, so a chat doesn't stop after one answer.
lessons.topic: Reactions ({{Talaga?}}, {{Grabe!}}, {{Ang galing!}}); follow-up questions with the right focus; {{E ikaw?}}, {{Ikaw naman?}}; {{mahilig}}

goal.tr: Really? How did you manage that?

dialog.t: Talaga? Ang galing! Paano mo nagawa iyon?
dialog.tr: Really? That's amazing! How did you manage that?

dialog.t: Nag-ensayo ako araw-araw sa loob ng anim na buwan.
dialog.tr: I trained every day for six months.

dialog.t: Siyempre napagod! Pero masaya. E ikaw, mahilig ka bang tumakbo?
dialog.tr: Of course I got tired! But it was fun. What about you, do you like running?

dialog.t: Hindi masyado. Mas gusto kong lumangoy.

blocks.p: In a Filipino conversation, an answer is an invitation. Keep it going in three ways: **react**, **ask more**, and **turn it back**.

**Follow-up questions use everything you know**: the question word first, the pronoun right after it, and the focus that fits what you ask about: {{Saan kayo kumain?}} “Where did you eat?” (actor focus), {{Ano ang kinain ninyo?}} “What did you eat?” (object focus), {{Sino ang kasama mo?}} “Who were you with?”
**Checking you understood**: {{di ba?}} turns a statement into “right?”: {{Taga-Davao ka, di ba?}}. {{Ibig mong sabihin…}} “You mean…”.
**Showing interest without a question**: {{Ah, kaya pala!}} “Oh, so that's why!”, {{Oo nga, ano?}} “That's true, isn't it?”, {{Sige, kuwento mo pa!}} “Go on, tell me more!”

ex.tr: Really? How did you manage that?

ex.t: E ikaw, mahilig ka bang tumakbo?
ex.tr: What about you, do you like running?

blocks.tip: {{mahilig}} “fond of, into” is the natural way to ask about hobbies: {{Mahilig ka bang magluto?}} “Do you like cooking?”, {{Mahilig ako sa musika.}} “I'm into music.”

mistakes.why: {{nagawa}} is object focus (the thing done is {{iyon}}): the doer is {{mo}}.
{{kasama mo}} is “your companion”: the {{ko}} set, like {{bahay mo}}.
